---
title: "Player Performance in Major vs. Non Major Tournaments"
editor: visual
---

<br>

This page continues to focus on the “Big 3” (Djokovic, Federer, Nadal) and the “New 2” (Alcaraz & Sinner). The plots included here look into player performance in different types of tournaments.

There are four major tournaments (Grand Slams) every calendar year, including the US Open, French Open, Australian Open, and Wimbledon. These are the most coveted and prestigious titles, due to a large pot of prize money, the most ranking points, and the global recognition that comes with winning them. Besides these Grand Slams, there are non-major tournaments almost every weekend. These include different levels of tournaments, including Master’s 1000s, 500s, 250s, etc. In the visualization below, we looked at how these five players’ titles are distributed between the two categories, and how their winning percentages compare to one another. 


```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
cleaned_rankings_data <- readRDS(file = here::here("data", "processed", "cleaned_rankings_data.rds"))
atp_singles_data <- readRDS(file = here::here("data", "processed", "atp_singles.Rds"))
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
source(here::here("major.R"))
```


<br>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.cap: " "
#| fig.align: "center" 
#| out.width: "800px"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "majorswinp.png"))
```

This visualization shows the difference between both categories for all five players. For all of them, the difference is extremely thin, being around a 5% increase in win percentage while playing in major tournaments. While it may be counter intuitive that these players have a higher win percentage in major tournaments, it likely signals that more competitive environments bring out the best from these five dominant athletes.

It also may be a phenomenon with the more talented players, as top ranked competitors have less of an incentive to participate in non-major tournaments being that they have already made a name for themselves. This would likely increase the amount of matches played within major tournaments especially during the prime of their careers. While the non-major matches were likely played early on, when the players were still figuring out the professional game and beginning to enter their primes.

The next visualization investigates the total number of tournaments that each player has won:

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.cap: " "
#| fig.align: "center" 
#| out.width: "800px"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "majortitles.png"))
```

This graph exhibits the number of total singles tournaments won on the y axis, as well as on the top of each bar. This graph is more intuitive, with each player racking up many more non-major tournament wins than major tournament wins. It is very interesting to note that all players have around a 1:3 or 1:4 major to non-major ratio, except for Jannik Sinner. 

Again, an important limitation of looking at total career patterns within this group of players is that the Big Three have a long and illustrious career, and a larger sample size to look at, while Sinner and Alcaraz are just beginning their careers. However, we can see from these visualizations that the “New 2” are already making significant strides at the beginning stages of their careers.
